lead: The Smith chart is graph paper for the reflection coefficient Γ = (Z − Z0)/(Z + Z0). It maps every normalized impedance z = Z/Z0 to a point inside a unit circle. A length of line becomes a circular arc, and VSWR (voltage standing wave ratio, the ratio of maximum to minimum voltage on the line) becomes a circle. Matching becomes an intersection. Engineers use it to read input impedance, VSWR, stub position and stub length without solving complex equations. It stays useful in RF labs and in CAD tools that draw the same chart on screen.
prereq: You need: reflection coefficient and VSWR from 1.2, input impedance from 1.3, and stub matching from 1.4.

sections.h3: The map from impedance to reflection coefficient

blocks.text: Normalize the load first. z = Z/Z0 = r + jx. Z is the load impedance in ohms, Z0 is the real characteristic impedance in ohms, r is normalized resistance, x is normalized reactance. Both r and x are pure numbers. A 100 + j50 Ω load on a 50 Ω line gives z = 2 + j1.

The reflection coefficient is Γ = (Z − Z0)/(Z + Z0) = (z − 1)/(z + 1). Γ is complex: Γ = Γr + jΓi. The inverse is z = (1 + Γ)/(1 − Γ). For a passive load |Γ| ≤ 1, so every point lies inside or on the unit circle.

Special points fix the chart. Short circuit z = 0 gives Γ = −1, the left edge. Open circuit z → ∞ gives Γ = +1, the right edge. Match z = 1 gives Γ = 0, the centre. Pure reactance r = 0 lies on the outer circle.
Constant r circle: centre r/(1+r), radius 1/(1+r). Constant x circle: centre 1 + j/x, radius 1/|x|.
blocks.where: r and x are normalized resistance and reactance; centres and radii are in the Γ plane.

blocks.text: Constant-r circles touch the right point Γ = +1. Constant-x arcs also pass through that point. The chart prints both families. Read r and x where the two curves meet.

Every point at the same radius has the same |Γ|. Therefore it has the same VSWR: VSWR = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|). A VSWR circle is centred at the match Γ = 0. Moving along a lossless line does not change |Γ|; the point only slides on this circle.

blocks.where: ΓL is the load reflection coefficient; d is the distance from the load toward the generator in metres; β = 2π/λ is the phase constant in rad/m; λ is the guide wavelength in metres.

blocks.text: The exponent changes phase by 2βd. The factor 2 appears because the wave travels d forward and d back. A full 360° turn needs 2βd = 2π, so d = λ/2. A λ/4 length turns the point by 180°. On a standard chart, moving toward the generator is clockwise.

Admittance uses the same chart. y = Y/Y0 = 1/z = g + jb. Here Y is admittance in siemens, Y0 = 1/Z0, g is normalized conductance, b is normalized susceptance. The admittance point is the impedance point rotated by 180°, because the admittance reflection coefficient is −Γ. Many charts also print admittance scales; do not mix the two readings.
Shunt stubs are easier on the admittance side. A shunt stub adds susceptance in parallel, so you need a point where the line admittance has g = 1. The stub cancels the remaining ±jb.

sections.h3: Using the chart to design a match

items: Plot Γ = (zL − 1)/(zL + 1), or locate zL directly on the chart.
Draw the VSWR circle through the point, centred at the match.
For a shunt stub, use admittance scales and move clockwise toward the generator until the point meets the g = 1 circle. Read d/λ on the outer wavelength scale; d is the stub position from the load.
At that point read susceptance b. The stub must supply −b. Read the short or open stub length from the chart or from the stub formula.

blocks.text: For a series stub, stay on impedance scales, move to the r = 1 circle and cancel x. Accuracy is limited by the printed grid. Use a sharp pencil, a compass and a large chart. Check the answer: d must lie between 0 and λ/2. For a short-circuited series stub of length l, the reactance is X = Z0·tan(βl), with X in ohms, l in metres and β = 2π/λ; the stub is shorter than λ/4 when it supplies positive (inductive) reactance. For a short-circuited shunt stub, the susceptance is B = −Y0·cot(βl), with B in siemens and Y0 = 1/Z0; the stub is shorter than λ/4 when it supplies negative (inductive) susceptance, and lies between λ/4 and λ/2 when it supplies positive (capacitive) susceptance.

figure.caption: The load 100 + j50 Ω on a 50 Ω line gives z = 2 + j1 and Γ = 0.4 + j0.2; the circle of constant |Γ| = 0.4472 carries the point as the line length changes.

spec.aria: The chart procedure normalizes a 100 + j50 ohm load to 2 + j1, plots reflection 0.4 + j0.2, draws the 0.4472 radius VSWR circle, rotates by 2 beta d and reads the match.

examples.question: A 50 Ω lossless line ends in ZL = 100 + j50 Ω. (a) Find normalized load zL. (b) Find Γ. (c) Find |Γ| and VSWR. (d) State where the point lies on the chart.
steps: Γ = (zL − 1)/(zL + 1) = (1 + j1)/(3 + j1). Multiply numerator and denominator by (3 − j1): numerator 4 + j2; denominator 10. Γ = 0.4 + j0.2.
The point is inside the unit circle at radius 0.4472; its VSWR circle has radius 0.4472. It is in the upper half because x = +1 is inductive.
examples.check:
Z0 = 50.0
ZL = complex(100.0, 50.0)
zL = ZL / Z0
G = (zL - 1) / (zL + 1)
print(round(G.real, 4))
print(round(G.imag, 4))
print(round(abs(G), 4))
print(round((1 + abs(G)) / (1 - abs(G)), 3))

traps: Plotting ZL in ohms directly: the chart axes are z = Z/Z0, so normalize by Z0 first.
Rotating the wrong way: distance toward the generator is clockwise on a standard chart; toward the load is anticlockwise.
Using |Γ| as VSWR: VSWR = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|), so |Γ| = 0.5 gives VSWR = 3.
Reading a shunt stub on impedance scales: convert to admittance y = 1/z, or use the 180° rotated point.
Treating a full turn as λ: one full 360° turn is λ/2; λ/4 is 180°.

quiz.q: Define normalized impedance on a Smith chart.
quiz.a: z = Z/Z0 = r + jx, where Z is load impedance, Z0 is characteristic impedance, r and x are normalized resistance and reactance.

quiz.q: Why does a lossless line move a point on a circle centred at Γ = 0?
quiz.a: Lossless line changes only phase of Γ: Γ(d) = ΓL e^(−j2βd). |Γ| stays constant, so radius and VSWR stay constant.

quiz.q: ZL = 100 + j50 Ω on a 50 Ω line. Find zL and Γ.
For Γ = 0.4 + j0.2, find |Γ| and VSWR.
Describe how to find shunt stub position and length on a Smith chart.
quiz.a: Normalize the load, plot Γ, draw the VSWR circle. Use admittance scales, move clockwise to g = 1, read d/λ. Read b there; the stub supplies −b. Read the short or open stub length from the chart or formula.

quiz.q: Why is the admittance chart the impedance chart rotated by 180°?
quiz.a: y = 1/z and the admittance reflection coefficient is −Γ. Multiplying Γ by −1 rotates the point by 180°.

quiz.q: What line length gives one full turn on the Smith chart?

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern RF design software draws the Smith chart and solves matching automatically, but the chart remains the quick check on a network analyser screen. It is used for impedance matching in phone front ends, antenna feeds and microwave test benches. Search for 'Smith chart admittance stub matching' and 'Smith chart normalized impedance circles' to go deeper.
